items.title: Roy Carew Interview, 1961-06-21
items.q: so he wrote out the chorus and handed it to me so i went and i struggled with it a while and i got words to the chorus and so i took it back to him... so we published the four songs

ctx.x: George K. and I, John Steiner, are interviewing Roy Carew at his home, 818 Quintana Street, Washington, D.C., on June, what's the date? 21st. We've talked briefly before we began about some of Roy's reminiscences, and in order to make this a little more logical to the listener, we'll ask Roy to tell us where and when he was born, something about his family and his earliest

musical inclinations. Well, it's a long time ago. I was born in Michigan, Grand Rapids, and on December the 15th, 1883, and now in my 78th year, my folks came to Michigan from Canada. My father's father, having emigrated from Somersetshire in England to Nova Scotia, then traveled west to Ontario, and my father and the remainder of the family moved over into Michigan in the 1880. I grew up in Grand Rapids when I was 17, and in my 18th year, really, I went to New York for a season, got a job, and earned my living…
The music as well as the words?

items.title: Roy Carew Interview, 1964-11-28
items.q: He asked me if I wanted to go down. ... So I told Jelly, I said, you join the union. ... I couldn't get them interested. I say, I wish I had really known the value of things as they turned out.

ctx.x: Well, did they have a, you said they had a, my home is in a southern town, was one that he did for Jazzmen?

Well, he made it the same time he was making these others. Oh, I see. Just another session down there. He asked me if I wanted to go down. I was just easing into knowing him, you know, and getting in touch with what was water around here. As I say, I wish I'd known more about it. And I, at that time, I, the word came up, you know, about if the man, if the recording artist didn't belong at the union, well, there would be a howl raised about issuing records made by him. So I told Jelly, I said, you join the union.…
Well, how did you ever get general records interested? Was that Charles Smith that got them started?

items.title: Roy Carew Interview, 1958-Fall
items.q: The interviewee discusses Jelly Roll Morton's musical interpretations and claims regarding compositions (e.g., 'Someday Sweetheart', 'Wolverine Blues') but does not describe a personal interaction, meeting, or professional collaboration with him.

ctx.x: That's, yeah, that's what it was that he was doing.

That was the, that was the, what gave Jelly the other, let Jelly know what I meant. He probably was playing a variation of it of his own. And, uh, went ahead and then he added a couple of parts when he did it for General Neckler record.

The, uh, you know, is there, I seem to have the idea that Johnny, the Jelly Roll wrote Someday Sweetheart. I mean, well, he said he did. He, well, in the, in the, in the, in the Library of Congress records, he says that, uh, something about Someday Sweetheart. He said the Spikesbugs wrote it anywhere that, with their names on it, so they must have written it. Finally. But somewhere else, somebody said that Jelly Roll, or maybe Jelly does himself.
